Stand

STAND · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Stand is a firmly held position or stance on an issue.

The senator's stand on water rights cost her votes in farming counties.

Worked Example

When the school board proposed cutting the art program, the principal took a public stand against the plan.

The principal declared a firm position on the issue and defended it openly -- 'taking a stand' means committing to a clear opinion and standing behind it.

How Strong Is It? — opinion → stand → conviction

opinion vs. stand

opinion vs. stand: An opinion can stay private and change by dinnertime -- a stand is a position you announce and defend.

conviction vs. stand

conviction vs. stand: A conviction is deeper than a stand -- a core belief so firm it shapes everything you do.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — stand

root — stand: to stay upright; to remain firm (standan) (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Stand is pure Old English -- standan, 'to stay upright, remain firm' -- a single piece with no prefix or suffix to peel off. The noun grew straight out of that image: taking a stand means planting your feet on an issue and refusing to be moved.

Use the root in a new word: standpoint

Use the root in a new word: standpoint: From the mayor's standpoint, the new stadium was worth every tax dollar.

Strength Check

Word Choice

On the ISEE, this stand means a declared position on an issue -- you take a stand, defend your stand, or ask about a politician's stand. It is not a physical spot, stall, or duty post: the guard's post and the fruit stand are different senses of the word.
